title: Multi-Society Clinical Practice Guidance on Perioperative Management of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists
journal: Multisociety consensus (ASA, ASMBS, ASRA, ISPCOP, SAGES)
breakthrough: Replaced rigid, time-based holding of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists — such as withholding weekly doses for 7 days — with dynamic risk stratification based on GI symptom screening and point-of-care gastric ultrasound (POCUS), plus shared decision-making about proceeding.
impact: Adopted across five societies, establishing a common algorithm for evaluating delayed gastric emptying and mitigating aspiration risk rather than a single hold interval.
practical: Eliminates unnecessary cancellations for asymptomatic patients on long-acting GLP-1 RAs, and brings bedside gastric ultrasound into the preoperative assessment when the holding interval cannot be verified.
link: Multi-society guidance on perioperative GLP-1 receptor agonists

verify.note: Was titled and dated as a 2025 ASA guideline. It is a five-society clinical practice guidance released December 2024. Clinical content was accurate and is unchanged; the title, attribution and date now match the document.

title: Long-Term Survival after Propofol or Sevoflurane Anaesthesia for Major Cancer Surgery: Follow-up of a Multicentre Randomised Trial
breakthrough: Long-term follow-up of a multicentre randomised trial in older patients undergoing major cancer surgery found no significant difference in survival between propofol-based total intravenous anaesthesia and sevoflurane-based volatile anaesthesia.
impact: No guideline recommends TIVA for oncologic benefit. The two trials designed to settle the question definitively — GAS TIVA (22 sites, non-small-cell lung cancer) and VAPOR-C (lung and colorectal, 2x2 factorial with lidocaine) — are still reporting, so the honest position is equipoise rather than a closed question.
practical: Choose the maintenance technique on hemodynamics, PONV risk and drug availability. The theoretical immunomodulatory argument for TIVA has no outcome data behind it.
link: British Journal of Anaesthesia - propofol vs sevoflurane, long-term survival

verify.note: The original cited a 2025 Lancet trial providing 'definitive' 3-year recurrence-free survival data. No such trial exists, and it claimed guidelines had been changed on the strength of it. Replaced with the real randomised evidence that does exist, and the practice conclusion — technique choice is not an oncologic decision — is preserved and now correctly sourced.

title: Individualized Perioperative Blood Pressure Management in Patients Undergoing Major Abdominal Surgery: The IMPROVE-multi Randomized Clinical Trial
breakthrough: A negative trial, and an important one. Individualized MAP targets set from each patient's preoperative mean nighttime MAP did NOT reduce the composite of acute kidney injury, myocardial injury, nonfatal cardiac arrest or death within 7 postoperative days, compared with routine management at a MAP target of 65 mmHg or higher, in patients at high risk of postoperative complications.
impact: Supports keeping the population-based MAP ≥ 65 mmHg threshold as the default rather than moving to personalized relative targets. The appeal of individualizing pressure to a patient's own baseline is intuitive, and this trial is the reason it has not become a standard.
practical: Treat MAP below 65 mmHg promptly, and do not invest in baseline-relative targets or predictive hemodynamic software on the expectation of an organ-protection benefit — that benefit has not been demonstrated in a randomized trial.
link: JAMA - IMPROVE-multi individualized blood pressure trial

verify.status: replaced — original stated the opposite result
verify.note: The original cited an 'HPI-SMART Trial' that does not exist, said it showed individualized relative MAP targets significantly reduce AKI and myocardial injury, and said international hemodynamic standards were rewritten to recommend targeting within 10-15% of baseline. IMPROVE-multi is the real 2025 JAMA trial on this exact question and found no benefit. The entry now states the actual finding.

title: ASA Practice Guideline for Monitoring and Antagonism of Neuromuscular Blockade
breakthrough: Established quantitative neuromuscular monitoring at the adductor pollicis, confirming a train-of-four ratio ≥ 0.9 before extubation, and held that subjective visual or tactile TOF assessment cannot rule out residual paralysis.
impact: Recommends sugammadex over neostigmine at deep, moderate and shallow depths of rocuronium-induced block, with neostigmine a reasonable alternative at minimal depth. Quantitative monitoring applies while giving the antagonist, not only before extubation.
practical: Facilities are fitting ORs with quantitative acceleromyography or electromyography and documenting a numerical TOF ratio before tracheal extubation. Residual block remains a live safety problem, which is what the guideline exists to address.
link: ASA - Monitoring and Antagonism of Neuromuscular Blockade

verify.note: Was presented as a new 2025 guideline. It is the ASA guideline published in 2023. Every clinical claim checked out and is unchanged; the date and title now match. Also softened 'mandated' to what the document does — it recommends.

title: Low versus High Intraoperative Fraction of Inspired Oxygen and Postoperative Organ Complications: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
breakthrough: Twenty randomized trials, 5,793 patients. Low intraoperative FiO₂ produced less atelectasis (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.63-0.97) but MORE acute kidney injury (RR 1.64, 95% CI 1.15-2.34). The tradeoff runs in both directions, which is why no single target has been adopted.
impact: Separately, a meta-analysis of 30 studies and 18,055 patients found high FiO₂ (mainly 80%) did not reduce surgical site infection versus low FiO₂ (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.79-1.03). That removes infection prevention as a justification for routine hyperoxia, but it does not establish a restrictive target in its place.
practical: Titrate to adequate oxygenation rather than leaving the blender at a high default, and understand what is being traded — atelectasis against kidney injury. No society has adopted a 92-96% intraoperative SpO₂ target, and the evidence does not yet support one.
link: Systematic review - low vs high intraoperative FiO₂

verify.status: replaced — original overstated a nonexistent trial
verify.note: The original cited a 2025 NEJM pragmatic trial proving intraoperative hyperoxia increases pulmonary complications, and said major societies had rewritten oxygen guidelines to a 92-96% SpO₂ target. No such trial was found and no such target has been adopted. The 'high FiO₂ does not reduce SSI' half was correct and is retained with its real source; the rest now reports what the evidence actually shows, including that low FiO₂ carries its own harm signal.

title: Elective Peri-operative Management of Adults Taking GLP-1 Receptor Agonists, GIP Agonists and SGLT2 Inhibitors: A Multidisciplinary Consensus Statement
breakthrough: Set a 3-day preoperative hold for sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors before elective surgery, and a pathway for evaluating ketosis — including blood beta-hydroxybutyrate — when the hold was not achieved.
impact: A multidisciplinary consensus spanning anaesthesia, endocrinology, surgery and pharmacy, giving one protocol for euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (eDKA) prevention across specialties. The consensus states plainly that there is no Class 1 evidence in this area, so it rests on expert agreement rather than trial data.
practical: Gives a structured approach for urgent and emergent procedures where the drug could not be held, including metabolic panel and blood ketone screening. Note that eDKA presents with a normal or near-normal glucose, so a reassuring fingerstick does not exclude it.
link: Anaesthesia - peri-operative GLP-1, GIP and SGLT2 inhibitor consensus

verify.note: Two errors fixed. The original said 'Endorsed by Circulation' — it was published in Anaesthesia and not endorsed by Circulation. And the hold is 3 days, not '3-4 days'. Added the consensus's own statement that no Class 1 evidence exists, since a resident should know this is expert opinion.

title: Restrictive versus Liberal Red-Cell Transfusion in Cardiac Surgery (TRICS III)
breakthrough: More than 5,000 adults at moderate-to-high predicted risk of death undergoing on-pump cardiac surgery. A restrictive threshold (transfuse below 7.5 g/dL from induction) was noninferior to a liberal one (below 9.5 g/dL in the OR, 8.5 g/dL on the ward) for the composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke or new dialysis: 11.4% versus 12.5%, within the prespecified 3% noninferiority margin. Transfusion rates were 52.3% versus 72.6%.
impact: Underpins the restrictive thresholds in current Patient Blood Management guidance for cardiac surgery, and the finding held at 6 months.
practical: Substantially reduces blood product use and the exposure that comes with it (TRALI, TACO), and eases blood bank demand, without a penalty in major morbidity or mortality.
link: NEJM - TRICS III cardiac surgery transfusion trial

verify.status: corrected — wrong trial name and year
verify.note: The original called this the 'TITRE-3 Trial' and dated it 2025 with a '90-day MACCE' endpoint. No trial by that name exists; the description is TRICS III, NEJM 2017. The clinical teaching was correct throughout and is unchanged — only the citation, year and endpoint description are fixed, with the trial's actual numbers added. title: Spinal versus General Anaesthesia for Hip Fracture Surgery: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Using a Consensus Core Outcome Set (REGAIN and RAGA)
breakthrough: Two large randomized trials settled this. REGAIN randomized 1,600 previously ambulatory patients aged 50+ across 46 US and Canadian hospitals: delirium did not differ by technique — 33.9% versus 37.8% in those with cognitive impairment, 16.2% versus 16.0% in those without — nor did ambulation or survival at 60 days. RAGA randomized 950 patients aged 65+ across 9 Chinese teaching hospitals and likewise found no difference in delirium.
impact: Regional anaesthesia is no longer recommended for neurocognitive protection in hip fracture surgery. Geriatric perioperative guidance has moved the emphasis to avoiding excessive anaesthetic depth and burst suppression, which is modifiable, rather than to the choice of technique, which is not the lever it was believed to be.
practical: Choose spinal or general on the patient's anatomy, hemodynamic tolerance and preference. Pain scores, length of stay and independent ambulation are also comparable, so there is no hidden cost to either choice.
link: British Journal of Anaesthesia - spinal vs general for hip fracture, meta-analysis

verify.status: corrected — wrong trial name and year
verify.note: The original cited a 2025 'RACE-2 Trial' in JAMA Surgery with processed-EEG-guided GA as the comparator. No such trial exists. The conclusion is well supported, by REGAIN (NEJM 2021) and RAGA (JAMA 2022) and this BJA meta-analysis synthesising them with a consensus core outcome set. Teaching preserved, citations corrected, real numbers added.

title: 2024 AHA/ACC Multisociety Guideline for Perioperative Cardiovascular Management for Noncardiac Surgery
breakthrough: Set out when to measure cardiac troponin around noncardiac surgery and how to act on it, replacing the 2014 guideline. Preoperative high-sensitivity troponin identifies chronic myocardial injury as well as patients at increased perioperative risk.
impact: Measuring cTn before surgery is reasonable in patients with known cardiovascular disease, or aged ≥ 65, or aged ≥ 45 with symptoms suggestive of CVD, undergoing elevated-risk noncardiac surgery. Endorsed by nine societies (AHA, ACC, ACS, ASNC, HRS, SCA, SCCT, SCMR, SVM).
practical: Detects myocardial injury after noncardiac surgery (MINS) in patients who never report chest pain, which is most of them. Detection is what triggers cardiology evaluation and secondary prevention — though the guideline does not claim a specific mortality reduction from screening itself.

verify.note: Three fixes. It is a 2024 full guideline, not a 2025 focused update. It is not joint with ESAIC — it is a nine-society US document. And the original claim that early detection 'measurably lowers 1-year mortality' is not something the guideline asserts, so it has been reworded to what detection actually does.

title: Viscoelastometric-Guided Early Fibrinogen Concentrate Replacement during Postpartum Haemorrhage (OBS2)
breakthrough: A negative double-blind randomized trial, and the reason early fibrinogen is not given empirically. Fibrinogen concentrate triggered by a FIBTEM A5 ≤ 15 mm did not reduce allogeneic transfusion: adjusted incidence rate ratio 0.72 (95% CI 0.3-1.7), P = 0.45. FIDEL likewise found no benefit from early systematic fibrinogen after vaginal delivery.
impact: Guidance continues to reserve fibrinogen replacement for measured hypofibrinogenemia during ongoing bleeding, rather than giving it early on a viscoelastic trigger. Viscoelastic testing earns its place by identifying which patients are actually hypofibrinogenemic — not by prompting routine early replacement.
practical: Use ROTEM or TEG to find true hypofibrinogenemia and treat that. The appeal of pre-emptive fibrinogen in obstetric hemorrhage is strong and has been tested twice; both trials were negative.
link: British Journal of Anaesthesia - OBS2 fibrinogen in postpartum haemorrhage

verify.status: replaced — original stated the opposite result
verify.note: The original cited a 2025 Lancet multicentre trial proving VHA-guided fibrinogen reduces ICU admissions and blood product exposure, and said obstetric hemorrhage standards now strongly recommend it over plasma. No such trial exists. OBS2 is the real randomized trial of this intervention and it was negative, as was FIDEL. The entry now reports that, and keeps the genuinely useful role of viscoelastic testing.
